newsitem.title: USA: A year later, TWA probers still seek cause.
newsitem.headline: A year later, TWA probers still seek cause.

text.p: A year after the crash of Trans World Airlines Inc's TWA Flight 800, the cause of the jet's mid-air explosion remains a mystery.
Investigators say they now strongly suspect that mechanical failure -- and not a terrorist missile or bomb -- destroyed the plane.
To those who lost loved ones, however, the answer scarcely matters.
"Whether they find a cause or they never find a cause, that won't have any affect on my feelings," said Frank Carven, whose daughter Paula and grandson Jay were killed.
Paula Carven, a TWA flight attendant, was taking her son to Paris as a gift for his ninth birthday on the ill-fated flight.

The Paris-bound Boeing 747 exploded on July 17, 1996, off the coast of Long Island, minutes after taking off from New York's Kennedy International Airport. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed.
Initially, many investigators felt certain the blast must have been caused by a criminal attack. Today, they are equally certain it wasn't.

"Because of the huge fireball, the lack of communication from the cockpit, no distress calls and so many people who saw an event in the sky, there seemed there was a good chance this was a criminal act of terrorism," Jim Kallstrom, who has headed the FBI's crash investigation, said in a recent interview.

Scores of people reported seeing streaks of light that appeared to be headed toward the plane seconds before it blew up. The plane's flight recorder, or so-called black box, showed no advance warnings of any problem.
Investigators now know that an explosion ripped through the jet's nearly empty, but vapor-filled, center fuel tank, but they do not know what caused the explosion.
"We've seen no evidence of a crime," Kallstrom said, "but we're still looking."
This week, investigators were flying test flights out of Kennedy airport, tracing the path of Flight 800 and hoping to replicate conditions on board the doomed plane.
A fresh team of metallurgists was re-examining about 200 holes, rips and tears in a reconstruction of the plane's center section in an airplane hangar in Calverton, New York.
Some 95 percent of the wreckage was retrieved from the 120-foot-deep ocean water by divers and trawling ships.
"We're on the last 2 or 3 percent of things left to do," Kallstrom said. "We're in the final stage of the criminal investigation."
He said he hopes to be able to give a final answer to the FBI's most pressing question -- was the explosion caused by a criminal act -- in 60 to 90 days.
"We're trying to be very, very certain," he said -- as he has many times since the investigation began.

Kallstrom has said the bomb theory fell from favor in the minds of many investigators after traces of PETN and other explosives were found on plane debris. The chemical residue proved to be left from a test of bomb-sniffing dogs on board the plane a few weeks before the fatal flight.
At times, Kallstrom has sounded frustrated and doubtful that any solution to the cause of the crash will be found. Lately he has been upbeat.
"It's possible we'll never know, but it's more likely we will," he said.
Frank Carven agreed.

"Everybody has said from day one that things like this just don't happen to 747s. Well, it happened, so there's got to be, there's an answer. Something caused it," he said. "I mean we're almost in the year 2000, and something doesn't happen without a reason. It's there. I'm sure it's there somewhere."
If no criminal act is found, the investigation into TWA Flight 800 falls wholly into the hands of the National Transportation Safety Board, which thus far has shared the responsibility with the FBI.

Even without a cause being found, the crash has brought changes. At U.S. airports, security has been drastically tightened, and a law was passed last year requiring airlines to release passenger lists quickly in the event of a crash.
